speaking.text: Most plants lose a portion of the carbon they fix because the enzyme responsible occasionally grabs oxygen instead. A minority of species evolved a preliminary step that concentrates carbon dioxide before the enzyme encounters it, and this modification allows them to thrive in hot, bright conditions where ordinary plants become inefficient.

Zero entered European mathematics late and met considerable resistance. A symbol for nothing seemed philosophically suspect, and several cities forbade its use in commercial accounts on the grounds that it was too easily altered. The objection was practical rather than mystical, and it delayed adoption by roughly two centuries.

Tall buildings became possible not when steel frames arrived but when someone made falling impossible. Elisha Otis demonstrated a brake that gripped the guide rails if the cable failed, and he did so by having the rope cut while he stood on the platform. Confidence, rather than height, was the obstacle.

The first synthetic dye was discovered by a student attempting to make a malaria treatment during a school holiday. The reaction failed and left a purple residue in the flask, and within a decade the colour had become a fashion across Europe, founding an industry that reshaped chemistry itself.

An ice shelf is not sea ice but the floating extension of a glacier, and its loss raises sea level almost not at all, because it was already displacing water. What matters is that the shelf acts as a buttress. Remove it and the land ice behind accelerates toward the ocean.

The Domesday Book recorded the ownership and value of almost every landholding in England within a single year. Its purpose was taxation rather than history, and the thoroughness that made it hated at the time is exactly what makes it the most complete portrait of any medieval society in Europe.

chart.title: Four writing systems compared
chart.summary: The table contrasts symbol count with survival. The two logographic systems have by far the most symbols, roughly a thousand and fifty thousand, while the two systems with about two dozen symbols are alphabetic or consonantal. Age does not predict survival: Chinese is over three thousand years old and still used, while Phoenician is younger than Egyptian and neither survives. Hangul is by far the youngest at AD 1443. A strong answer compares symbol count against type, notes that survival does not track age, and identifies hangul as the only deliberately designed system in the set.

lecture.transcript: I want to tell you about a piece of statistical reasoning from the Second World War, because it is the clearest illustration I know of a mistake that is very hard to see from the inside. The American military wanted to add armour to its bombers. Armour is heavy, so you cannot armour the whole aircraft; you have to choose. They examined aircraft returning from missions and mapped where the bullet holes were, and the holes clustered on the wings, the fuselage and the tail gunner's position. The obvious recommendation is to reinforce the areas with the most damage. Abraham Wald, a statistician working with the Statistical Research Group, pointed out that this was precisely backwards. The data consisted only of aircraft that had returned. Damage was distributed fairly evenly across the fleet; what differed was which damage let you come home. Holes in the wings appeared frequently in the sample because a plane hit in the wings could still fly. There were almost no returning aircraft with holes in the engines, and the reason was not that engines were rarely hit. It was that a plane hit in the engine did not come back to be counted. So the armour should go where the holes are not. Now, the general form of this error has a name, survivorship bias, and once you have the concept you find it everywhere: in studies of successful companies that never examine the failed ones, in advice from people who took a risk and prospered, in any dataset assembled from whatever happened to survive. The bias is not in the numbers. It is in the selection of what got measured, and no amount of care with the arithmetic will reveal it.
key: the military wanted to armour bombers but could not armour everything, so had to choose
bullet holes on returning aircraft clustered on wings, fuselage and tail
the intuitive recommendation was to reinforce the damaged areas
Wald saw the sample contained only aircraft that returned; engine hits were absent because those planes did not come back

the general error is survivorship bias, arising from selection of what was measured rather than from the arithmetic

lecture.transcript: Today I want to trace how the public library became a normal institution, because the arguments made against it are instructive. In the eighteen forties, when the first legislation was debated in Britain, opposition was substantial and it was not primarily about cost, though cost was mentioned. Three objections recur in the record. The first was that reading would be a distraction from labour, and that a working population with access to books would be less inclined to accept the hours it was expected to work. This objection was made openly, which tells you something about the period. The second was that free provision would destroy the commercial circulating libraries, which were numerous, profitable and worked reasonably well for anyone who could afford a subscription. That objection was accurate; they largely did disappear. The third was subtler and has aged least well. It held that a collection assembled by a committee and paid for from the rates would inevitably reflect the tastes of the committee, and that a public library would therefore be an instrument of instruction rather than a resource. What actually happened was that public demand pushed the collections toward fiction, which the founders had explicitly hoped to exclude, and by the end of the century novels made up the majority of borrowing in most towns. I find that reversal worth dwelling on. The institution survived by becoming something other than what its advocates intended, and the thing they were most anxious to prevent turned out to be what made it popular enough to keep funding.

swt.passage: Goodhart's law is usually stated as the observation that a measure ceases to be a good measure once it becomes a target, and its explanatory reach is wider than its origin suggests. Charles Goodhart was writing about monetary policy, noting that statistical relationships the Bank of England relied upon broke down as soon as policy was set to control them. The mechanism generalises because it does not depend on anyone acting dishonestly. Any indicator is a proxy: it correlates with the thing actually wanted because both are produced by the same underlying process. Once effort is directed at the indicator specifically, the correlation is broken, since the indicator can be raised by routes that leave the underlying quality untouched. Hospitals judged on waiting times have reclassified patients rather than treated them faster; schools judged on pass rates have moved pupils away from subjects they might fail; police forces judged on detection rates have concentrated on offences that are easy to detect. In each case the workers responded rationally to the instruction they were actually given. The practical implication is uncomfortable for anyone designing an accountability system, because it suggests that the better a measure is at capturing quality, the more damage is done by making it a target, and the measures safest to publish are those nobody is rewarded for improving.

swt.passage: William Baumol observed in the nineteen sixties that a string quartet requires exactly the same four musicians and the same forty minutes to perform a Beethoven quartet as it did in 1800, while a factory worker's hourly output has risen many times over in the same period. Productivity growth in manufacturing raises wages across the whole economy, because employers in every sector must compete for labour, and this means the cost of activities where productivity cannot rise increases relentlessly in relative terms. The effect is not a failure of management and cannot be fixed by working harder. It applies to any activity whose output is the labour itself: live performance, teaching, nursing, hairdressing, social care. Two consequences follow. The first is that the share of national income spent on such services must rise over time even if their quality and quantity are unchanged, which is routinely misreported as a crisis of spiralling costs. The second is that pressure to raise measured productivity in these sectors usually amounts to reducing the service, since the only way to make a nurse cover more patients per hour is for each patient to receive less. Recognising this does not solve the funding problem, but it clarifies what is actually being decided.

reading.passage: The distinction between weather and climate is understood well enough in principle and collapses constantly in public argument, usually because both sides make the same error in opposite directions. A cold week is offered as evidence against warming; a heatwave is offered as evidence for it. Neither is admissible on its own, because climate is the distribution from which weather is drawn, and a single observation tells you very little about a distribution. What has changed is that attribution science now permits a more careful version of the second claim. By running large ensembles of climate simulations with and without observed greenhouse gas concentrations, researchers can estimate how much more likely a particular event has become. The output is probabilistic rather than categorical: a given heatwave might be assessed as ten times more probable than in a pre-industrial climate. This is a genuine advance and it is routinely reported as though it established that warming caused the event, which is a stronger and different claim. Careful communication of the distinction has proved harder than the science it describes.

reading.passage: Historic building conservation has moved away from restoration and toward repair, and the reasoning behind the shift is worth stating carefully. Nineteenth-century restorers routinely returned buildings to an imagined original state, removing later additions and replacing weathered stonework with crisp new carving in the same style. The result looks coherent and destroys evidence: a wall that has been recut no longer records how it was built, what it was repaired with, or what happened to it in between. Modern practice treats the building as a document whose later chapters are as informative as its first. Repairs are therefore made to be identifiable on close inspection, using compatible but distinguishable materials, and later additions are retained unless they are actively causing harm. The approach frequently disappoints visitors who expect a finished appearance, and it preserves the one thing a replica cannot supply.
reading.q: What is the central principle of modern conservation described here?
options: A building is treated as a record whose later alterations carry evidence worth keeping.
Buildings should be returned to their original appearance wherever documentation allows.
Repairs should be made invisible so that the structure appears unaltered.
Later additions should be removed to restore stylistic coherence.

reading.passage: Economists have long puzzled over why people buy extended warranties, since the products are, on any reasonable actuarial analysis, poor value: the premium substantially exceeds the expected cost of repair, and the buyer is generally able to absorb that cost without hardship. Insurance makes sense for losses that would be ruinous, which is precisely why it makes little sense for a washing machine. The most persuasive explanation is not that consumers cannot calculate. It is that the purchase occurs at the moment of maximum anxiety about a decision already made, and what is being bought is relief from the possibility of having chosen badly. The retailer's margin on the warranty frequently exceeds the margin on the appliance, which explains why the offer arrives at the till rather than in the advertising.
reading.q: How does the author explain the popularity of extended warranties?

Consumers lack the arithmetic to evaluate the expected cost of repair.
The premiums are correctly priced against the true likelihood of appliance failure.
Retailers are legally required to offer them at the point of sale.

listening.transcript: I want to work through a piece of arithmetic that has real consequences in medicine, and that almost everybody, including many clinicians, gets wrong the first time. Imagine a screening test for a disease that affects one person in a thousand. The test is good: it correctly identifies ninety-nine per cent of people who have the disease, and it correctly clears ninety-five per cent of people who do not. You take the test and it comes back positive. What is the probability that you have the disease? Most people answer somewhere between ninety and ninety-nine per cent. The correct answer is about two per cent. Here is why. Take a hundred thousand people. One hundred of them have the disease, and the test catches ninety-nine of those. The other ninety-nine thousand nine hundred do not have it, and the test wrongly flags five per cent of them, which is roughly five thousand people. So among everyone who tests positive, ninety-nine have the disease and five thousand do not. The overwhelming majority of positives are false, not because the test is bad, but because the healthy group is so much larger that even a small error rate applied to it produces more false positives than there are true cases. This is called base rate neglect, and it is not a curiosity. It is the reason mass screening for rare conditions can do net harm: every false positive leads to further investigation, which carries its own risk, and to a period of considerable fear. The test has not failed. The failure is in reasoning about a rare condition as though the population were evenly divided, and no improvement in test accuracy removes the problem while the base rate remains low.

the healthy group is so much larger that a small false positive rate produces more false positives than true cases
in a hundred thousand people, roughly ninety-nine true positives against five thousand false ones
the error is called base rate neglect and is common among clinicians too

I want to say something about the claim that medieval people believed the earth was flat, because it is almost entirely a nineteenth-century invention. Educated Europeans knew the earth was spherical throughout the middle ages; the fact is stated plainly in standard textbooks of the period, and the objection to Columbus was never about shape. It was about size. His critics thought, correctly as it happens, that he had badly underestimated the circumference and would run out of supplies long before reaching Asia. He survived because an unexpected continent was in the way. The flat earth story was popularised by writers in the eighteen seventies who were constructing a narrative of conflict between science and religion, and it has proved remarkably durable because it flatters the present at the expense of a period nobody defends.

listening.transcript: One thing about writing up results that costs people marks every year. When an experiment does not work, the temptation is to describe it briefly and move on to whatever did work. Resist that. A negative result that has been carefully obtained is a finding, and describing exactly what you did and why it failed is often the most useful thing in the report, because the next person will otherwise repeat it. What loses marks is not failure; it is a report in which the failure is mentioned in a sentence and the reader cannot tell whether the method was flawed or the hypothesis was wrong. Those two possibilities require completely different follow-up work, and distinguishing them is most of what the write-up is for.
listening.q: What does the speaker say about experiments that do not work?

The measure costs very little and has been slow to spread mainly because planning rules specify colour

Rivers carry more sediment than water in some seasons, and the Yellow River takes its name from precisely this. The load is so heavy that the bed rises as silt is deposited, and centuries of embankment building have left long stretches flowing above the surrounding plain. A breach in such a river does not merely flood the land beside it; the channel may abandon its course entirely and reach the sea hundreds of kilometres away.
